event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers to the 2026 international armed conflict centered on Iran, the United States and Israel, with effects extending across the Persian Gulf and neighboring states. U.S. combat operations began on February 28, 2026; the conflict has also made security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz a central issue.

facts.label: Start date
facts.value: The United States notified the UN Security Council that it commenced combat operations against Iran on February 28, 2026; U.S. energy officials likewise identify military action on that date as the point after which Hormuz traffic was effectively disrupted.

facts.label: Principal parties and stated U.S. purpos
facts.value: In its UN notification, the United States said it was acting in cooperation with Israel, citing protection of U.S. forces and regional partners and the free flow of maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz. These are the U.S. government's stated objectives, not an independent legal finding.

facts.label: Legal position asserted by the United St
facts.value: The United States characterized its operations as necessary and proportionate self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including collective self-defense of Israel.

facts.label: Why the Strait of Hormuz matters
facts.value: The strait lies between Iran and Oman and links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. In the first half of 2025, about 20.9 million barrels per day of oil—roughly one-fifth of global petroleum-liquids consumption—moved through it, while alternative routes could replace only part of disrupted flows.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers chosen developments on July 22-23, 2026—including military threats, U.S. war-powers action and oil-market effects—and does not attempt to provide a complete account of the conflict, diplomacy, or humanitarian consequences.

event_overview.title: About Iran Conflict
event_overview.subject: Iran Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Iran Conflict refers here to the 2026 direct military confrontation between the United States and Iran, which has expanded beyond Iranian territory to include attacks and claimed attacks on U.S. forces, partner states and maritime activity in the Middle East. The confrontation has centered in part on control and security of the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran’s reported retaliatory operations have involved missiles and drones directed at regional sites hosting U.S. personnel.

facts.label: Start of the direct conflict
facts.value: Reporting describes U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, as the start of the present direct war; it is distinct from the longer-running U.S.-Iran rivalry and regional proxy conflicts.

facts.label: Ceasefire and renewed fighting
facts.value: The United States and Iran reached an interim arrangement or ceasefire in mid-June 2026, but reporting says the truce subsequently broke down amid a confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz and renewed U.S. and Iranian attacks.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: The conflict’s military and economic effects extend across Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and neighboring states that host U.S. facilities, including Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan; reports of individual strikes and damage may be contested or unverified.

facts.label: Why Bahrain and Kuwait matter
facts.value: Bahrain hosts U.S. Naval Support Activity Bahrain and the U.S. Fifth Fleet/NAVCENT presence, while Camp Arifjan in Kuwait supports Army prepositioned stocks and theater sustainment for U.S. Central Command operations.

facts.label: Maritime dimension
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a central theater because it is a strategic shipping chokepoint; the U.S. Fifth Fleet’s area of responsibility includes the Arabian Gulf and the strait, alongside other regional waterways.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows selected 2026 escalations involving U.S.-Iran military and maritime actions, including reported attacks affecting U.S. regional facilities, rather than documenting every diplomatic, proxy, domestic or historical aspect of U.S.-Iran relations.

event_overview.title: About US-Saudi Nuclear Deal
event_overview.subject: US-Saudi Nuclear Deal
event_overview.summary: The event concerns a U.S.-Saudi agreement for peaceful nuclear cooperation, commonly called a “123 agreement,” signed on July 22, 2026 alongside a bilateral safeguards agreement. It establishes a legal framework for potential U.S. civil-nuclear exports and commercial participation in Saudi Arabia’s nuclear-energy program, while making nonproliferation, safety and security central stated objectives.

facts.label: Parties and date
facts.value: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement and an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement on July 22, 2026.

facts.label: Legal framework
facts.value: The accord is a Section 123 agreement under the U.S. Atomic Energy Act of 1954—the mechanism used for significant civil nuclear cooperation, including NRC-licensed exports of nuclear material, reactors, equipment and components.

facts.label: Congressional process
facts.value: The Department of Energy said the agreement would be transmitted to Congress for review; standard Section 123 agreements are subject to two review periods totaling 90 days of continuous congressional session before they may enter into force absent enacted disapproval.

facts.label: Stated purpose
facts.value: DOE describes the arrangement as supporting U.S. access to Saudi nuclear-energy opportunities and Saudi energy needs, while advancing nuclear safety, security and nonproliferation objectives.

facts.label: International safeguards context
facts.value: Saudi Arabia’s comprehensive safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency has been in force since January 13, 2009; its Small Quantities Protocol was rescinded effective December 31, 2024.

facts.label: Storm classifications
facts.value: A tropical storm has maximum sustained winds of 39–73 mph; a hurricane has maximum sustained winds of at least 74 mph. Major hurricanes are Category 3–5 systems, beginning at 111 mph.

facts.label: Forecasting authority

event_overview.title: About Netanyahu Arrest Warrant
event_overview.subject: Netanyahu Arrest Warrant
event_overview.summary: The Netanyahu arrest-warrant event concerns an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Court’s Situation in the State of Palestine. The warrant has become a focus of debate over the ICC’s jurisdiction, the alleged crimes identified by the Court, and whether national or local authorities can or must act if Netanyahu travels abroad.

facts.label: Warrant date and court
facts.value: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu on November 21, 2024, in the ICC’s Situation in the State of Palestine.

facts.label: Allegations at the warrant stage
facts.value: The Chamber found reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu was responsible for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts. These are allegations supporting a warrant, not a conviction.

facts.label: Underlying investigation
facts.value: The ICC Prosecutor opened the Situation in Palestine investigation on March 3, 2021; it covers alleged Rome Statute crimes committed since June 13, 2014. The Court had held that its territorial jurisdiction for this situation extends to Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

facts.label: Jurisdiction dispute
facts.value: On November 21, 2024, the same ICC chamber rejected Israel’s then-pending jurisdiction and notification challenges, stating that Israel’s acceptance was not required for the Court to exercise territorial jurisdiction based on Palestine and that the jurisdiction challenge was premature at that stage.

facts.label: Enforcement framework
facts.value: The ICC does not itself carry out arrests; arrest powers rest with states. States Parties to the Rome Statute have obligations to cooperate with ICC arrest-and-surrender requests, while the United States is not a party to the Rome Statute.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows New York City political and legal statements in July 2026 about possible action on the ICC warrant; it does not attempt to chronicle the full ICC case, the Gaza war, or all international responses to the warrant.

event_overview.summary: The event concerns the July 2026 U.S. arrest of Andrew and Tristan Tate after UK prosecutors sought their extradition to face criminal charges in England. It is an extradition and charging matter, not a finding of guilt: the Crown Prosecution Service says the proceedings are active and that guilt can be determined only by a court.

facts.label: Arrest and location
facts.value: The brothers were arrested by the U.S. Marshals Service in the United States on July 18, 2026; reporting and the selected timeline identify Miami, Florida, as the location of the arrest.

facts.label: UK charging scope
facts.value: The CPS said it would pursue extradition on 21 pre-existing charges and further charges involving four additional alleged victims. The added allegations include rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, assault, and offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.

facts.label: Alleged time period and victims
facts.value: According to the CPS, the further alleged offending occurred between July 2010 and August 2017; the charging decisions brought the stated total number of alleged victims in the UK case to seven.

facts.label: Earlier extradition history
facts.value: UK extradition warrants were issued at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in January 2024. In March 2024, the Bucharest Court of Appeal ordered extradition to the UK only after separate Romanian criminal proceedings concluded.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: The CPS requested extradition from the United States, and as of July 19, 2026 said the brothers had been arrested and were awaiting extradition proceedings. The CPS emphasizes that a charging decision is not a finding of fact or guilt and that the defendants have a right to a fair trial.

event_overview.title: About UK Prime Minister Transition
event_overview.subject: UK Prime Minister Transition
event_overview.summary: This event is the July 2026 transfer of leadership of the UK government from Keir Starmer to Andy Burnham after Starmer resigned and Burnham became Labour leader. Burnham formally took office on 20 July 2026, when he accepted King Charles III’s invitation to form a government; reports dated 21 July cover his first full day in office rather than a separate constitutional swearing-in.

facts.label: Effective date
facts.value: Andy Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026; the UK Parliament records his premiership as beginning that day.

facts.label: Transfer of office
facts.value: Keir Starmer said he was resigning on 20 July 2026, and Burnham stated that he had accepted the King’s invitation at Buckingham Palace to form a government.

facts.label: Constitutional basis
facts.value: The prime minister is head of the UK government and holds office by being able to command the confidence of the House of Commons; political parties determine and communicate who is best placed to do so, after which the Sovereign appoints the successor.

facts.label: Political and parliamentary position
facts.value: Burnham was elected Labour leader in July 2026 and is the Labour MP for Makerfield, elected in June 2026.

facts.label: Office and responsibilities
facts.value: As prime minister, Burnham is also First Lord of the Treasury, Minister for the Civil Service and Minister for the Union; the prime minister leads His Majesty’s Government and is ultimately responsible for government policy and decisions.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate July 20–21, 2026 leadership handover and Burnham’s assumption of office, not the full Labour leadership contest, Starmer’s wider record, or subsequent actions of the new government.

facts.label: Attack pattern
facts.value: Long-range missiles and drones used by Russian armed forces have been a major driver of civilian harm, particularly in urban areas away from the front line; short-range drones are also a major source of casualties near front lines.

facts.label: International monitoring
facts.value: The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine was deployed in March 2014 and publicly monitors and reports on the human-rights situation, including civilian casualties, across the country.

facts.label: International legal context
facts.value: On March 16, 2022, the International Court of Justice indicated provisional measures ordering Russia to suspend the military operations it had commenced in Ukraine; the order stated that it did not decide the Court’s jurisdiction or the merits of the case.

event_overview.title: About Cockroach Movement Protests
event_overview.subject: Cockroach Movement Protests
event_overview.summary: The Cockroach Movement is a youth-led Indian protest movement organized around the self-styled Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). It began as online satire in May 2026 and developed into street protests focused on alleged examination irregularities, education reform, unemployment and government accountability; supporters have specifically called for the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

facts.label: Origins and status
facts.value: The CJP emerged online in May 2026 and had become an active, ongoing protest movement by July 21, 2026 rather than a formally established political party or a time-limited event.

facts.label: First major street action
facts.value: Its first reported public street demonstration took place in New Delhi on June 6, 2026, moving the campaign from social media into in-person protest.

facts.label: Organization and participants
facts.value: The movement is associated with the Cockroach Janta Party and its founder, Abhijeet Dipke; it is chiefly youth- and student-led, while later protests also drew professionals and families.

facts.label: Stated aims
facts.value: Its central demands concern accountability for alleged failures in India’s examination system and education reform, including a demand that the education minister resign; the movement also frames unemployment and broader government accountability as concerns.

facts.label: Examination context
facts.value: The protests arose amid controversy over NEET (UG) 2026. The National Testing Agency officially conducted a re-examination on June 21, 2026 and issued fee-refund notices for candidates from the original May 3 examination.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the New Delhi confrontation of July 20, 2026 and protesters’ stated intention to continue on July 21; it does not attempt to catalog the movement’s full online origins, every local protest, or all examination-related proceedings.

event_overview.title: About World Cup 2026
event_overview.subject: World Cup 2026
event_overview.summary: The FIFA World Cup 2026 is the 23rd edition of FIFA’s men’s national-team football championship. It is the first World Cup jointly hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, and its expanded field and knockout structure culminate in a final on July 19, 2026.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The tournament runs from June 11 through July 19, 2026.

facts.label: Hosts and venues
facts.value: Canada, Mexico and the United States are co-hosting the competition across 16 host cities; this is the first World Cup shared among three countries.

facts.label: Organizer and participants
facts.value: FIFA organizes the tournament, which has a record 48 participating national teams and 104 matches.

facts.label: Competition format
facts.value: The 48 teams are divided into 12 groups of four. The top two in each group and the eight best third-place teams advance to a Round of 32, followed by single-elimination rounds, including a third-place match and final.

facts.label: Concluding matches
facts.value: The third-place match is scheduled for July 18 at Miami Stadium, and the final is scheduled for July 19 at New York New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the tournament’s closing-stage developments on July 18-19, 2026, rather than the full qualification process, group stage, or every match in the competition.

events.summary: Laos officials have stated that they cannot determine the cause of deaths of tourists linked to methanol poisoning due to the absence of autopsies.
